rv.q: “Is This a Room,” which opened on Monday at the Lyceum Theater, turns the ums and stutters and bizarre non sequiturs of recorded speech into astonishing — and astonishingly emotional — theater.
The note-perfect production simply leaves no space for extraneous imaginings.
Nevertheless, a 65-minute verbatim transcript has now become the basis for one of the thrillingest thrillers ever to hit Broadway.
The show goes down like a thriller, and should be a commercial no-brainer.
In Tina Satter’s eerie, essential play about the NSA-leaker Reality Winner, the nature of everything seems to waver.
“Is This a Room” in its understated way expresses with full-throated clarity something seriously out of whack in our political system.

Davis gives a performance of heart-wrenching rawness and lucidity; as you watch her dissolve from the inside, what emerges with force is a sympathetic and specific portrait of a young woman trying to do the right thing in a very wrong time.
It’s a fascinating piece in every way, replete with fabulous central performances from both Emily Davis (who plays Winner) and Pete Simpson (who plays the lead FBI agent at the interrogation).
The play just sort of starts and ends, without fanfare or adornment, and yet, in its heightened presentation of reality, emerges as one of the most radical works on Broadway.
Is This a Room feels like a breath of fresh air in the commercial theater realm.

For already making that unsettling Trump administration accomplishment perfectly clear, Satter deserves many thanks.
Her play is not about the reality of Reality Winner but the surreality of modern existence, so much of which keeps us in the dark.
But I think by not telling the whole story, “A Room” is almost as guilty as Winner of letting the American people down.
It’s a visionary work that will certainly help put documentary theater back on the map, while also making us question what is even real.

cn.t: Critics praise this verbatim FBI transcript as a surprisingly gripping psychological thriller, with Tina Satter's direction transforming 65 minutes of documentary material into taut, anxiety-inducing drama led by Emily Davis's compelling performance.

vs.sum: The Lyceum Theatre offers good sightlines and a charming Beaux Arts ambiance, but suffers from cramped seating and small restrooms. Ideal for intimate dramas, but patrons should be prepared for less comfort during their visit.

acc.note: 4 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. No elevator. Infrared devices available.
